FOIA is that all public records are open to all citizens of the Commonwealth of Virginia. The purpose is to be transparent and that any citizen, if they have a question or they need information, they can readily receive it. So who does this apply to? A public body. Now, a public body is in the traditional sense, the school board or the board of supervisors at the county, but

it also includes committees. So any committee that's of the school board, that the school board either creates as an advisory committee, a standing committee, or a select committee. So you all, MSAC, are considered a committee of the school board and therefore a public body. So we're going to go over a few quick things, and we're going to leave plenty of time for questions. So required trainings. In general, whenever someone becomes a member of a public

body, they have to receive a copy of the Virginia Freedom of Information Act, and there's also different trainings depending on your level. So school board members have to have more formal trainings, while committees often receive this type of presentation as a training. It's important that you familiarize yourself with what's required in FOIA because you are members of a public body, you are also subject to the requirements of FOIA. So meetings. Meetings are considered an assemblage of

three or more members of a committee. If you have a committee that is less than three, then two would be your quorum. So what constitutes a meeting? It's any time you're discussing public business. So in the context of MSAC, it would be any time you're discussing an item that requires you to advise the school board. So a lot of times you all provide advice on policies or on regulations.

That would be considered transacting business, or the business of MSAC. So there's certain requirements for meetings with respect to whether or not you can have a virtual meeting or if you can attend electronically. I recommend that you check out Policy 2420 because there are very specific requirements. As a general matter, unless it's a public emergency, most meetings will be in person. But there are certain requirements for medical concerns or other issues that

may allow you to participate remotely. Here, there's a caution against simultaneous electronic communications. There are several court cases that have said if there's a huge group of a committee and they're all in one big chat together, that can be construed as a public meeting. And why is that important? Because that means you're discussing information and there's no record of it. So if a member of the public wanted to know what you all were discussing, they would not have access to that information.

So it's important for members of the public to know when a public body is meeting and what is being transacted during that meeting. So some of the steps that we recommend for people is not replying all to an email blast. If you receive an email from a member of the committee and it goes out to everyone, that's great. It's a one-time communication. But when people start replying all and engage into a large discussion on email, it can be considered simultaneous

communication. So try whenever possible to keep your communications one-on-one. Phone, or if you want to use your email, make sure you're using it for public business, and I'll get into why that is in a minute. That means that they can receive that information subject to certain exemptions, which are all set out in the Virginia Freedom of Information Act. The first timeline is five days.
